newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Payday for Kabul's civil servants.
newsitem.headline: Payday for Kabul's civil servants.

text.p: Throughout the Afghan capital civil servants were counting huge piles of 50 Afghani banknotes on Sunday. They had just received their first pay in two months.

Fifty Afghanis is worth a third of a U.S. cent. The average monthly pay of a civil servant in the Afghan capital is 102,000 Afghanis, or $6. Senior staff members earn the equivalent of between $12 and $15 a month.

Analysts of the Afghan situation in Kabul say they suspect the cause of both the late payment and the small denominations is that the ex-government of Burhanuddin Rabbani took most of the contents of the central bank with them when they fled Kabul.

The analysts say the currency is not printed in Afghanistan and suggest that until the Taleban are recognised as the rightful government, they will have difficulty persuading the printers to provide them with more currency.
The Taleban have yet to be recognised at the legal government in Afghanistan by any foreign country.

The government was one of the main sources of the cash that kept the ravaged economy stumbling along. What little industry Kabul had was devastated by four years of civil war. Factories on the western edge of the city are mainly roofless hulks.
But there is even doubt that Sunday's injection of cash will help the economy on the road to recovery. Many shopkeepers will not accept the notes for anything but the smallest purchases.
Money changers nn the market charge 20 per cent to change the notes into 5,000 and 10,000 Afghni notes.
Kabul's economy has suffered an unprecedented slump since the Taleban took over the city in late September, in part because of the lack of government spending.

"This is the worst time I can remember." shopkeeper Mohammed Naim Tahiri said. "In the past people could manage to work part time despite being employed by the government. NOe they are being squeezed. From one side the pay is irregular and from the other, there is no work."
"No one has any money. This is the worst time I can remember in my eight years of business." Tahiri added.

Hardware dealer Mohammed Haidar paints a bleak picture for Kabul's small shopkeepers. "Living conditions are not good for most people, and those who are left only have enough money to buy food." he said.

Even food is expensive in Kabul. For years the city laboured under a blockade and the little that did get through from Pakistan or the north of the country was subject to savage "taxes' levied by the numerous checkpoints along the road.
Although the Taleban have removed the checkpoints and the price of basic foodstuffs has fallen, they are still too expensive for the city's poorer residents.
Ismael Omer of the United Nations World Food Programme has the job of trying to relieve their hardship. "Although food is abundant in Kabul, it is not affordable to everybody." he told Reuters.

The economic situation in the city has been exacerbated by the Taleban's policy towards women. The number of men either killed or otherwise unavailable for employment because of the civil war meant that women -- who traditionally had little economic influence in Afghanistan -- had carved out a major role for themselves.
The loss of almost half the work-force has hit Kabul's economy hard.
As the civil servants headed out of the ministries clutching their packages of 50 Afghani notes on Sunday, they were heading into a bleak economic future.
